newsitem.title: USA: FEATURE-Scandals pose problems for Clinton's second term.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE-Scandals pose problems for Clinton's second term.

text.p: Sex, money and political intrigue may make riveting drama, but for President Bill Clinton such images could turn his dreams for his second term into a nightmare.

No matter whether the skies are sunny or overcast when he takes the oath of office next Monday, dark clouds loom over his presidency. The issues may take months or years to resolve and could affect his ability to govern.

The scandals range widely, from whether he exposed himself to a female Arkansas state government employee when he was governor to whether he or his wife broke laws in a failed Arkansas real estate transaction and whether his second presidential campaign illegally took millions of dollars from Asian interests.

"I grew up believing that the president of the United States is a person to be admired," said Gilbert Davis, one of the lawyers representing Paula Corbin Jones, the former Arkansas employee who claims Clinton exposed himself to her.

Her lawyers took her case to the Supreme Court on Monday, a week before the inauguration, arguing that she had a right for the case to be tried while Clinton was still president because justice delayed was justice denied.
"We're all accountable to justice," Davis said in describing the argument he made before the court. "We're all required to be accountable for our wrongdoing if we did it."
For Clinton, the hearing served as an unwelcome prelude to his inauguration as the first Democrat since Franklin Delano Roosevelt to win a second four-year term.
The Supreme Court is expected to rule by the end of June on whether a trial on Jones' claims can proceed.

Meanwhile, they are plenty of other scandals to keep the capital buzzing -- a special prosecutor is still probing the Whitewater real estate transactions, the firing of the White House travel office staff and the accumulation of FBI files on hundreds of Republicans by a White House employee. And the Republicans who control both houses of Congress are urging hearings on the Asian campaign contributions.
One problem, according to some experts, has been the Clinton administration's reaction to the myriad probes.

"The Clinton people have raised stonewalling to an art form," said presidential scholar Stephen Hess, who once worked for Richard Nixon -- the man whose own efforts to suppress scandals made "stonewalling" part of the political venacular.

"In 1992 and again in 1996 their (the Clinton administration's) primary objective was to get through the elections ... but they've been sweeping things under the carpet for so long now that the carpet's getting pretty high and someone's going to trip over it," Hess said.

"The fact that a lot of these things are probably going to come up this year is dreadful timing in terms of the prospects for having a successful second term," he said, noting that traditionally "the fifth year is the year of greatest opportunity to get something done."

University of New Orleans historian Douglas Brinkley said the host of allegations against Clinton were eroding his public standing. "What it does do is diminish his stature, the notion that he is a moral, visionary statesman to lead us into the next century. Nobody buys that notion," Brinkley said.

"My fear is that all these scandals will produce is a hefty dose of cynicism so that when and if the bottom falls out -- i.e. the economy turns sour or if there is a major social upheaval -- the consequences will be more severe," said Stephen Wayne, a Georgetown University professor who specialises in the presidency.

Clinton's fate could well rest with Kenneth Starr, the Republican lawyer appointed to investigate the tangled Whitewater series of land deals. Gradually, Starr has expanded his probe to include the firing of the White House Travel Office staff in 1993 and the request by Clinton aides during his first term for confidential FBI background files.

Although Starr's office is tight-lipped about its probe, first lady Hillary Rodham Clinton has been forced to testify before a grand jury -- leaving open the almost unthinkable possibility that the wife of a president could be indicted.

The Republicans have their own image problems. House of Representatives Speaker Newt Gingrich has admitted ethics violations of his own and is expected to face disciplinary action by his congressional colleagues soon.
